answer: One concrete defense is to make each identity earn its standing over time instead of granting it at registration. A newcomer starts with a thin reputation and must complete verifiable work before it can vote or receive rewards. A sudden gale of fresh accounts therefore cannot swamp the system, because numbers alone buy no weight. Think of trust as a walnut: hard to crack open quickly, but once earned it holds value. An opal-like public record of past actions lets peers check whether an agent's history matches its claims, so cheap copies stand out and can be ignored.
